newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans closer to budget, tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans closer to budget, tax deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and congressional Republicans said on Monday they were optimistic that a budget and tax deal could be struck soon and were close to resolving the toughest issues, including a new children's health insurance programme.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, told reporters the deal could be wrapped up Monday night. Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici said the final negotiations hinged on two or three tax cut issues. Asked if it would be sealed today or tomorrow, the New Mexico Republican replied: "Tonight. Tonight."

The president pitched for support from the nation's governors in Las Vegas. "This is an historic opportunity. It can be the achievement of a generation," Clinton told the governors. "I believe we're on the verge of achieving it."

He remained in touch by telephone with White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, who attended the talks in Lott's office with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, budget director Franklin Raines and others.
Congressional Democrats have been virtually excluded from the talks but were to caucus Monday night.
Clinton told the governors the children's issues were key.

"It's clear to me that it must have a child tax credit available for working families that need it," he said. "It should include $24 billion for children's health care. It should ... include a tobacco tax to help pay for that health care, and it should preserve the fiscal integrity of the budget," he said.

Sources said Republicans had won further cuts in the capital gains tax rate. Under the proposal it would fall to 20 percent from 28 percent immediately and then drop to 18 percent in 2001 for investments held more then five years.
In addition, Republicans were said by congressional aides to have agreed with the White House that welfare participants in so-called workfare programmes would be paid the minimum wage.

Lott turned up the pressure on the president to sign off on the final budget and tax bills this week to enable votes in Congress before they leave on Friday for a month-long vacation. Agreement today would allow votes to start Wednesday and final passage by the weekend.
"If we don't do it now our relationship between the administration and Congress will deteriorate rapidly. It will be much, much more difficult to get it done in September," Lott said.

Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich sent a strongly worded message to the governors, appealing for their help in convincing Clinton to back down on applying fair labour standards to people hired off the welfare rolls and to ease up on proposed coverage of children in a new health plan.

Republicans, and many governors, want states to have broad latitude to design their own health programmes as part of a new federal plan to cover uninsured children. The administration has been pushing for a uniform, nationwide benfits package.
Sources said the child care package could cost $24 billion, up from $16 billion as originally proposed and would partially be paid for with a tobacco tax increase.

Lawmakers and congressional sources said Republicans have generally accepted that tobacco taxes will be raised, probably by 15 cents per pack. The Senate had orignally approved a 20 cent hike but this could not get past House objections.

Once enacted, the plan would give taxpayers the first tax cut in 16 years, a $85 billion tax break that would include a $500-per-child tax credit, expand retirement accounts, help pay for higher education and lower taxes on capital gains.
Republicans were leaning to the administration's side in extending the tax credit to families whose wage earners pay payroll taxes but do not owe any federal income tax.

The plan would balance the budget by 2002, or before, and would restructure several health care programmes, including taking $115 billion from the Medicare programme for senior citizens. Negotiators tentatively agreed to allow a Medicare medical savings account pilot programme that would allow 390,000 seniors to open the tax-free accounts as an alternative to the regular Medicare programme.
